transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. Um... well, I guess I'm here mostly because my husband asked me to come. He and... well, some of the folks at the warehouse where I work, they keep acting like I'm, you know, making things up or acting crazy. 

I really don't want to sound like a difficult employee, I promise I'm a hard worker, but... I just know they've been watching my every move on the floor. And they keep changing my pallet counts to keep me from getting that supervisor spot. I'm just trying to do my job and do it right, you know? I hope it's alright that I'm telling you this... does that make sense?
Can you tell me how long you've felt that your coworkers have been watching you and changing your pallet counts—has this been going on for days, weeks, or longer?

Well, um... I guess it's been a little while. I don't want you to think I'm making a huge deal out of nothing, because I really do try to just put my head down and do my job. But... maybe about eight months? 

That's when I first started noticing them watching me and messing with the counts. And, um... I'm a little embarrassed to say this, please don't think I'm crazy, but... that's also when the voices started. Just, you know, hearing them say things about me even when no one is standing right there. 

So the voices and the feeling that they're changing my stuff... yeah, it's been about eight months now. I really try not to let it bother me at work, I promise. Is it okay that I'm telling you all this? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.
Over these past eight months, have you also noticed periods where your mood was very low, hopeless, or unusually high and energetic, separate from the voices and suspicions?

Um... well... I wouldn't say I get super low or hopeless. I really try to stay positive, you know? Keep a good attitude for my family and my job. But... I guess there are times when I feel... really energized? Like, um, fired up, I guess you could say. Like nobody can slow me down and I can just get everything done at once. 

I hope that doesn't sound like a bad thing. It's just... sometimes when I feel like that, I get a little, um, short-tempered. Like if my husband just asks me one small question about the kids or what my schedule is for the week, I just... I snap at him. It feels like he's trying to control me or get in my way when I'm on a roll. I always feel terrible about it later, I really do. I'm trying to be better about not snapping. Does that... is that the kind of thing you were asking about? I want to make sure I'm answering your questions right.
When you feel that 'fired up' and energized, how long does that feeling typically last—just a few hours, or does it continue for several days in a row?

Um... well, it definitely lasts longer than a few hours. I hope that's normal... I don't want to sound like I'm completely out of control or anything. But, um, those stretches where I feel really wired and, you know, I barely sleep but I still take on way too much at work and around the house... they usually last for several days at a time. 

And, um, I guess I've been having those kinds of stretches coming and going for about six months now? I try really hard to just channel all that energy into getting my work done, I promise I'm not just running wild. But yeah, it goes on for days. Is that... is that helpful? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of details.

Do you notice the voices and the feeling that coworkers are watching or changing your counts even during times when you're not feeling that 'fired up' energy—like when your mood is more normal or even low?

Um... yeah. Yeah, I do. I hope that doesn't make me sound too crazy, but... even when I'm not feeling all fired up, it's still there. 

Like, um, recently I had a few weeks where things were quieter? I was sleeping closer to normal, maybe getting six or seven hours, and I wasn't racing around trying to do a million things at once. I was just trying to be a good employee and a good mom, you know? But... even then, I still heard the voice. Just telling me I need to check things. And I still knew, I just *knew*, that they were changing the pallet counts to make me look bad. 

So, um, yeah, it doesn't just happen when I'm energized. It's kind of... always there in the background. Is that... does that make sense? I hope I explained that okay. I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need to figure this out.

Thinking back over the whole eight months, how much of that time would you say you were having the voices or suspicious thoughts without any of that 'fired up' energy or low mood at all—just a few weeks total, or more like half the time or more?

Um... well, if I'm looking back over the whole eight months... I guess I'd say the energized, fired-up times actually took up a lot of it. I hope that's okay to say. Like, for more than half of that whole time, I've had those stretches where I barely need to sleep and I'm just tackling everything, taking on all these extra tasks. 

And, um, that's when I get a little irritable if someone tries to slow me down. I try so hard not to be, but it just happens. So, yeah, the fired-up periods have been going on for a majority of the time, even though the voices and the pallet stuff are there too. Is that... is that the kind of timeline you were looking for? I really want to make sure I'm explaining it right.

latest_inference.note: Manic-like symptoms (elevated energy, decreased sleep, irritability, grandiosity) have been present for the majority of the 8-month illness course, yet psychotic symptoms (voices, delusions of surveillance/sabotage) persisted for several weeks in the absence of any mood disturbance. This pattern—concurrent mood and psychotic symptoms for most of the illness plus a distinct period of psychosis without mood symptoms—fits schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, and effectively rules out schizophrenia alone, since mood symptoms are too prominent and persistent to be considered incidental.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient describes ~8 months of persistent auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions (coworkers surveilling her and altering pallet counts) that occur both during and independent of mood disturbance. She also reports discrete manic-like episodes (elevated/irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, increased energy and goal-directed activity, irritability with functional consequences) lasting several days at a time, recurring over about 6 months and comprising more than half of the total illness duration. Critically, she endorses a period of several weeks with normal sleep and mood during which the voices and paranoid conviction persisted, establishing that psychotic symptoms occur in the absence of mood episodes for at least 2 weeks, while mood symptoms are present for the majority of the illness course. This pattern—concurrent major mood episode with psychosis, plus psychotic symptoms present for ≥2 weeks without mood symptoms, with mood symptoms predominating over the total illness duration—meets criteria for Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type (F25.0), rather than a primary mood disorder with psychotic features (F31.2) or schizophrenia (F20.9), where psychotic symptoms would need to persist for a substantial period without any mood component.
